#3182. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

#3181. Prediction: Micron Stock Is Going to Soar After Its December Earnings Report

The report could show whether Micron's rough autumn was a gift.

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›

Colette Kress has had a whirlwind week. Last Thursday, she went from Nvidia's (NVDA -3.12%) longtime finance chief to its interim chief executive officer after CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned. On Nov. 18, after Nvidia posted results, she told CNBC something every memory investor should hear: "What we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together."

Memory is Micron Technology's (MU -5.35%) whole world, and the Nvidia drama has helped drag Micron’s stock far below this year's high. That's why I'm circling Micron's next earnings report, due in December, on my calendar. Micron hasn't announced the exact day yet, but last year it reported its fiscal first-quarter results on Dec. 17.

The report will cover the first quarter of a year Micron's leaders have hyped for months. "As strong as fiscal 2026 was, we expect fiscal 2027 to be even better," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in September, adding that supply and demand should be "much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026."

The bigger reason December matters is what comes after it. Micron has already locked in most of its 2027 supply of high bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked chips that sit right beside artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processors, at significantly higher prices. Those prices "reset at the beginning of the calendar year," Micron President Manish Bhatia said. That means the guidance Micron gives in December will be the first to bake in those new prices. That forecast matters more to me than the quarter itself.

The quarter has a soft spot. Micron paid every employee a bigger bonus for 2026, and Chief Financial Officer Mark Murphy said much of that cost hits now, calling fiscal Q1 "the floor for gross margins in fiscal 2027." A dip is expected, and I'd only worry if the outlook for the next quarter doesn't improve.

I also want to hear how Micron's newest chips are selling. Micron is in high-volume production of HBM4 chips built for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, and Nvidia said that Vera Rubin systems have started shipping. Next up is a custom version co-designed with Nvidia, which Micron technology chief Scott DeBoer called "the first major custom HBM product out in the market."

That closeness cuts both ways. If Nvidia's leadership shake-up slows its orders, Micron feels it fast. Micron also has the smallest market share of the three big HBM makers, and rivals SK Hynix (SKHY -3.34%) and Samsung (SSNLF +0.00%) are building huge new factories in South Korea.

Micron has spent the year locking customers into multiyear supply deals. It has signed 26, and customers have backed them with $32 billion in commitments, mostly cash deposits. Partners include General Motors (GM -0.29%) and Ford Motor Company (F +3.47%), and Micron struck a separate strategic deal with Claude maker Anthropic. "The AI revolution has permanently elevated the role of memory and storage solutions from the data center to the edge," said Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana. New deals in December would tell me customers aren't flinching.

Shareholders could get more, too. Starting Dec. 9, limits on buybacks tied to Micron's federal CHIPS Act funding ease up. "Over time, we expect to return 100% of our excess cash to shareholders," Murphy said. December's call should show how hard Micron plans to lean in.

Then there are the factories, which is where I get a little nervous. In Taiwan, where most of Micron's DRAM came from in 2026, Micron has all but halted construction of a new memory plant amid a drawn-out labor dispute, according to Bloomberg.

Memory has always been a boom-and-bust business, and every new fabrication plant in the semiconductor industry brings the day when supply catches up to demand a little closer. For now, Mehrotra says, "We do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance."

If December shows 2027 prices sticking, customers still signing, and Nvidia's turmoil staying inside Nvidia, I think Micron's rough autumn will look like a buying opportunity.

#3180. What You Can Pay for with Scholarship Money

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Scholarships are usually restricted to the necessary costs of attending college, but some scholarships let you apply the money to more than tuition.

Scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university. This often includes required bills and purchases, such as tuition, textbooks and on-campus living expenses.

Some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition. How you can apply the money may depend on the scholarship’s requirements.

Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.

Scholarships commonly pay toward the tuition and fees your college charges.

Tuition usually covers only the cost to enroll in classes. Your college will also charge fees for a variety of reasons, such as attending a lab portion of a class, access to on-campus technology, facility maintenance and student activities. You’ll have to pay many of these fees regardless of if you use those facilities or participate in campus activities. Fees are often charged with tuition on the same bill so that you pay them together.

Tuition and fees cost students at public four-year institutions an average of $32,730 for the 2026-2027 school year, according to College Board’s 2026 report. If you use scholarship money to pay for these costs upfront, it can help you save a good chunk of money.

Scholarship money also pays for textbooks and supplies you need to complete your courses. These can include physical books, e-books and software licenses to access online content.

Depending on the scholarship, the cost of additional supplies that are required for certain courses might be covered as well. For example, nursing students might have to purchase scrubs with their college’s logo or medical supplies such as stethoscopes for clinical shifts.

Some scholarships will pay for the purchase of a laptop because you’ll likely need one to complete your coursework; however, you’ll want to confirm that the money can be used for that purchase before buying one.

Your scholarship might help cover some of the costs of living on campus, including paying for a dorm room and meal plans (often called room and board). To apply the funds, you usually have to live in university housing, which might be in a dormitory or even university apartments.

Many students can purchase meal plans to eat meals in their college and university cafeterias. These plans are usually for a set number of meals each week and might be required for first-year students. Because meal plans are part of college expenses, some scholarships will let you apply the funds to purchase a meal plan.

Some scholarships might also allow money to pay for campus parking fees because those are paid directly to the college or university.

» MORE: What is need-based financial aid for college?

Scholarships are generally intended only for educational expenses such as those explained above, but there are some scholarships that want you to use the money for specific expenses. If your scholarship has this type of restriction, your award letter should outline how the funds must be used, such as paying for tuition and fees only.

If you aren’t certain whether there are restrictions on how you can spend your scholarship money and the scholarship was paid directly to your college, you can call your financial aid office to ask. But you’ll want to contact the organization that awarded you the scholarship to ask about restrictions if the scholarship money was sent to you instead.

Even if a scholarship is open to most educational costs, expenses that are rarely allowed to be covered by a scholarship include:

Some transportation costs such as car payments.

Non-essential supplies such as clothing or entertainment.

Scholarships can be paid directly to your college or to you, depending on the individual scholarship. If the money goes to your college, it’s applied to your account based on the scholarship’s requirements. For example, if the funds are only allowed to pay for tuition, the financial aid office will apply the money to your tuition bill to reduce how much you owe.

Scholarships work the same way for room and board. If your scholarship will pay toward the costs of living on campus, the money will reduce how much you owe or cover the costs entirely so that you don’t owe anything.

In some cases, you might be able to use your scholarship money to pay for books or supplies. If that’s allowed, the funds might be available on your account through the college bookstore. Instead of paying the entire cost of your textbooks with cash or your student loans, you can pay with the scholarship money.

If your scholarship sends you the money instead of giving it to your college, you’ll be responsible for using the funds to pay for eligible costs instead of your university automatically applying it toward your bill.

#3179. ​2027 Prediction: Security Will Shed Its Reputation As The Bottleneck

Prashanth Harshangi is co-founder of Enkrypt AI, building security and governance infrastructure for enterprise AI deployments.

Security has a reputation problem. Ask almost any engineering leader what slows down an AI agent rollout, and you’ll hear some version of “waiting on security.”

I predict that in 2027 this reputation will flip. Security never slowed transformation. The real blocker is not knowing the answers to basic questions: Where does this agent run? What data can it reach? Who approved its tools, and what happens if one of them changes?

When no one can answer quickly, projects stall. A recent research report from Anaconda found that two-thirds of respondents had a deployment delayed by security concerns. Builders wait while security scrambles to reconstruct answers that should have existed from day one, until each side decides the other is the problem.

The real bottleneck is missing evidence, visibility and shared tooling. In 2027, organizations that build security into the foundation will turn it from a gate into what lets teams move faster with confidence.

A typical multi-week security review is mostly evidence-gathering: an inventory of models, versions, tools and data sources; testing against adversarial prompts and data leakage; and documentation mapped to frameworks like the NIST AI RMF or the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

That evidence takes the form of concrete artifacts: an up-to-date inventory of AI components, red teaming results tied to a specific build, logs of what an agent accessed and when and a record of which policies are enforced at runtime.

In 2027, more organizations will automate this work. When evidence is generated continuously in the pipeline, the review shrinks from weeks of archaeology to a short conversation about the few risks that need human judgment.

AI intensifies the speed-versus-security debate for two reasons.

First, the software supply chain now has a second layer of models, MCP servers and agent skills, often pulled in within a single afternoon. Many organizations track code dependencies carefully but can’t say which MCP servers their agents call. I expect the next wave of incidents to start with those untracked assets.

The early record already points that way. At our company, we maintain the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a public database of 570 source-verified security and safety events involving AI agents from 2022 to 2026. In 219 of them, a real party suffered real consequences, not just a researcher proving an attack was possible.

Second, agents can act as an insider that is neither human nor malicious. Picture a support agent connected to a customer database through an MCP server. A ticket arrives containing hidden instructions, and the agent follows them, pulling records it was never meant to share into its reply. Nothing was hacked in the traditional sense. The agent used permissions it already had, in a way no one anticipated.

The most useful mental model I’ve found, and one I expect leading organizations to adopt in 2027, is to treat an AI agent like a new hire. It gets an identity, a named human owner, a documented purpose and an approved tool list before it touches production. It receives the minimum permissions its job requires, scoped to the task and time-bound, never a copy of its owner’s full access. When it’s retired, its credentials are revoked and its activity record is preserved.

Static, role-based permissions can’t keep up with agents that choose tools at runtime and act on someone else’s behalf. Authorization will have to become contextual: What is this agent trying to do, for whom, right now—and is that within policy?

And when something goes wrong, “the AI did it” isn’t an answer. The human owner is accountable for the agent’s scope, the platform team for its controls and the organization for its policy.

Guardrails feel like a tax when they arrive late, block without explanation and require a ticket to get past. They feel like infrastructure when they’re built into the platform and tell developers why something was stopped and how to fix it.

My test is whether the secure way is also the easiest. If a developer can spin up an agent with preapproved models, vetted MCP servers and default guardrails in the time it takes to wire things up manually, most will choose the secure path without being asked.

In 2027, I expect automated red teaming in CI, configurable runtime guardrails and self-updating inventories to move security work out of the review meeting and into the tooling.

Toolchain checks will join them. Every MCP server and agent skill should be scanned before an agent can call it, the same way code dependencies are scanned before a merge.

That same report from Anaconda found that only 26% of teams reported having a highly unified AI toolchain. In 2027, having experienced the drawbacks of a disparate stack, the most effective CISOs, CTOs and CPOs will stop treating AI security as a handoff between teams and start treating it as a shared product.

That means shared metrics, such as time from agent prototype to approved production, tracked alongside incident and policy-violation rates. It means a single inventory of models, tools and agents that both teams trust and security engineers embedded with builders from the first design discussion, not the last review. And it means policies expressed as automated checks, so they stop being debates and become part of the build.

The organizations with the fewest controls won’t win the race. The winners will build controls into their infrastructure, so that shipping a secure agent is simply the default.

#3176. I Didn’t Know Southwest Points Could Be This Valuable

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Some of the best Southwest redemptions are only available if you hold one of the airline’s credit cards.

In a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary. But travel brands are pushing back against that narrative, offering exclusive perks and redemption packages to those who carry their cards.

Take Southwest Airlines, for example. Its Rapid Rewards loyalty program allows you to redeem points for flights, but it also offers a special program called Rapid Rewards Access Events exclusively for Southwest credit cardholders. In exchange for a decent chunk of points, you can get a vacation package that’s worth significantly more than the price you pay. Instead of a traditional flight award redemption, you get a cohesive travel experience.

"Experiences create lifetime memories,” says Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards. “For us, we really want them to have great memories and remember our brand as part of that.”

Southwest invited me to participate in one of its Rapid Rewards Access Events. While Southwest covered the cost of my trip, these opinions are my own. Here’s what I learned.

Every event is different (ranging from concerts to multiday trips), but big-ticket Rapid Rewards Access Events tend to include flights, hotel accommodations, meals and excursions.

The event I participated in was in Maui to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Southwest and Chase’s partnership. This was a bigger production than the typical event, with about 60 cardholders (and a plus one) participating. A typical multiday event might have 20 or 25 packages for sale.

In exchange for 275,000 Rapid Rewards points, cardholders received for themselves and one guest:

A four-night stay in an ocean-view room at the Grand Wailea, a Waldorf Astoria Resort, in Maui, including daily breakfast.

Ground transportation between the airport and the resort, as well as for any scheduled group activities.

A special welcome reception and farewell dinner.

A snorkeling cruise with lunch and beverages included.

A choice between several excursions, including a spa treatment, golf, ziplining and more.

Even at extremely conservative estimates, I would value all of those things at roughly $4,600. That’s $750 more than what NerdWallet values 275,000 Rapid Rewards points at, according to our 2026 data. If we took a more liberal approach, I think it would be fair to say the package was worth more than $7,000. That puts this redemption between 1.7 and 2.5 cents per point. (Expand the section below to see how I arrived at those numbers.)

As of 2026, NerdWallet values Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.4 cents apiece. That puts the 275,000-point Southwest event package at $3,850.

Let’s put some numbers to the package inclusions and see how the points price stacks up to the cash valuation.

$1,000 Southwest gift card: It’s pretty easy to value a $1,000 Southwest gift card at $1,000. You need to fly to the event, so that can be taken at face value. (You could also use it toward a different trip, if you wanted to use points or fly with a different carrier.)

Four-night hotel stay: For the Grand Wailea stay, a nonrefundable Hilton Honors discount rate for an ocean-view room on the exact same dates in 2027 costs $4,490.19, after factoring in taxes and fees. (The base-level terrace-view room would cost $3,992.17.)

If you were to use points, a standard room without an ocean view would cost 130,000 Hilton points per night. An ocean-view room’s rate shoots up to 281,000 Hilton points per night.

Using NerdWallet’s 2026 valuation of Hilton points at 0.4 cent per point, that puts the value of the two rooms at $2,080 and $4,496, respectively. To make things interesting, let’s say the hotel stay is worth $2,080.

Daily breakfast at the hotel buffet is about $60 per person, before tax and tip. For four days, let’s put that at around another $500, bringing the total stay value to $2,580.

Ground transportation: Let’s make things simple and just say it’s $30 each way between the airport and the resort. For two people, that would be worth $120.

Welcome reception and farewell dinner: Southwest and Chase put a lot of effort into making these events nice, from the food and free-flowing alcohol to the entertainment (there was even a fire performance at the farewell dinner).

I would value this at $50 per person, conservatively, or $200 total.

Snorkeling cruise: I went on Viator to find a similar experience, and the cheapest option I found was priced at $100 per person.

Again, let’s price it conservatively and say it’s worth $200. That price doesn't include hotel transportation, gratuities, towels or alcoholic beverages, while the Southwest package did.

Excursion choice: Southwest let everyone choose an excursion, ranging from a chill pool or spa day to ziplining through the jungle or learning to surf.

It’s hard to put a number on this, because the activities varied in cost.

I went ziplining, and it was $240 for six lines. That price doesn’t include transportation to the excursion, which was covered by Southwest. Meanwhile, a standard massage at the hotel spa is $275 (and that doesn’t even factor in the 20% service charge).

Let’s put this at $250 per person, giving us a round $500 for two people’s excursions.

Grand total: Summing up these numbers gets us $4,600. That’s $750 more than the $3,850 NerdWallet values 275,000 points at, but keep in mind that we probably undervalued several of the inclusions. The actual value of a trip like this could be much higher.

It also doesn’t factor in other things, like snacks provided at the hospitality booth, as well as surprise gifts and goodie bags prepared by Southwest and Chase for attendees.

Before you book a Rapid Rewards Access Event, there are some drawbacks to booking a vacation this way.

The biggest one is if you don’t like group trips or following a schedule on your vacations. Given the nature of these events, you’ll be surrounded by a group of travelers, many of whom will likely be longtime Southwest flyers. If you prefer to keep to yourself, then this type of trip is likely not a good fit.

You’ll also have multiple scheduled activities on your itinerary. While you can choose to not show up, those activities add a lot of value to the trip.

With that said, I found the itinerary quite laid back. The amount of scheduled activities wasn’t overwhelming, and there was plenty of free time to do whatever you wanted. One couple I met even rented a car and explored Maui in their downtime, so they kept themselves busy.

These events are extremely popular, and many attendees I met at the Maui event had been on multiple Southwest cardmember trips.

Scoring a ticket to a Rapid Rewards Access Event might even require setting your alarm for when tickets drop. Several cardmembers told me they’ve experienced times when the event they wanted was sold out in hours, if not minutes. (The Maui one took a few hours to sell out, because it was larger than most.)

Finally, 275,000 points is a lot — even if you're getting great value. If your Rapid Rewards points are collecting dust in your account, then it could make sense. But if you have a transferable currency, then you'd have to weigh whether you might get better value elsewhere, such as booking round-trip business class flights.

Southwest isn’t the only airline or travel brand to offer special events for cardholders. United Airlines has MileagePlus Exclusives and United Card Events from Chase; Delta Air Lines offers cardmember-exclusive redemptions in its SkyMiles Experiences program; and Marriott has its Marriott Bonvoy Moments program.

But every redemption option is different — even if it’s within the same loyalty program. For example, some Rapid Rewards Access Events are packages you can purchase immediately for a set price, while others are auction-style listings. Some programs offer paid experiences, so you can only pay in cash, not points.

Personally, I’m a fan of the fixed-price points option. You know the upfront price, and you don’t have to worry about getting into a last-minute bidding war that could lead you to paying more than you intended. Plus, Southwest has historically had limited award redemption options, although that will change in 2027 when it allows international partner award bookings.

Ultimately, whether you think a Rapid Rewards Access Event is a worthwhile redemption will depend on your interests, and Southwest is working to expand its offerings to meet people’s passions.

"We do offer a lot of breadth because we want to get different types of customers engaged with different types of things based on their individual passion points and what they're really interested in,” says Suri, the Rapid Rewards chief.

If you’d rather spend time in the mountains than on the beach, you might not want to spend 275,000 Rapid Rewards points on the Maui package.

Instead, you probably would've been interested in the 250,000-point package for "Boots, Bourbon and Bonfires" — a three-day trip to Devil's Thumb Ranch, an upscale dude ranch resort about 1.5 hours outside of Denver.

Before you book, just remember: You’ll need a Southwest credit card to purchase.

#3175. Letter To The CEO: AI Decisions You Cannot Delegate

Madhu Shashanka is the Cofounder, Chief Scientist and CTO at Concentric AI and author of the forthcoming book, Coherence.

For thirty years, the fastest company usually won. That era is ending, and most CEOs have not noticed.

AI is making execution cheap. Building a workflow, analyzing a market, drafting a contract: work that once required scarce talent and real time now takes a goal and an instruction. When your team can build almost anything in an afternoon, and so can every competitor, speed stops being an advantage. Everyone has it.

So what becomes scarce? Coherence: whether the growing crowd of autonomous systems inside your company, and the people accountable for them, still pull in the same direction. It is the one advantage a competitor cannot buy, because no vendor sells it. Capability, by contrast, is commoditizing. Your rivals will soon run the same models you do, at the same price, so an AI strategy built on having better tools is built on eroding ground. What does not commoditize is the capability to deploy all that intelligence coherently: data trustworthy enough to reason over, calibrated knowledge of which systems to rely on for what, the judgment to know which complexity your company can absorb. You only build those over years, which is why a competitor cannot close the gap by switching vendors.

Most companies are building the opposite. Execution got cheap, so everyone builds more. Sales stands up an agent, finance automates forecasting, operations wires up logistics. Each works. Each passes its own tests. On paper, the company gets more automated every quarter, and quietly harder to run, because two agents now act on contradictory assumptions, decisions flow through systems no one fully understands and every team sharpens its own corner while the whole loses its shape. This is complexity debt, and you cannot see it on any dashboard. You feel it later, as the sense that nobody can quite explain why the organization behaves the way it does.

I learned the underlying lesson the humbling way, long before agents existed. Early in my career, I built a data visualization I was proud of: dense, elegant, the kind of thing that impresses engineers. Users hated it. It was correct at the level I cared about and useless at the level that mattered. A system can be flawless at its task and still make the organization worse. Task-level success and enterprise value are different things, and most companies measure only the first, one agent at a time, across the whole enterprise.

This lands on your desk because the fix isn’t technical. Your Chief AI Officer can build the discipline. Only you can decide the company will live by it. Four acts are yours alone.

Set the risk appetite. How much unreviewed autonomy the company will accept, and in which domains it will never let a system act without a human, is a statement about your institution’s identity, not a technical parameter. The organization calibrates to it whether you say it out loud or not. So say it out loud.

Protect the function that can tell you no. Whatever coherence capability you build will, by design, sometimes block a business-unit head who wants to ship, a revenue line that wants to move and occasionally you. The organization learns whether that function is real not from the org chart but from what happens the first time its judgment constrains you. Accept a no you had the power to override, and you teach the company that coherence is not ceremonial. Route around it, and you teach the opposite—whatever the documents say. This single act decides whether any of it survives contact with the organization.

Hold the capital rule: build the judgment now, rent the plumbing later. The tools that monitor and permission autonomous systems are becoming cheap commodities you should buy. The judgment about what to deploy, decline and reverse is the asset, and it must be built inside your company. Holding that line against the pressure to build bespoke versions of what the market will soon sell cheaply is capital allocation—your defining act.

Reward the right thing. An organization optimizes the metrics its CEO asks about in reviews. Celebrate how many systems shipped, and you get deployment counts and the incoherence they generate. Ask whether the company can still see what its systems are doing and still recover when one fails, and you get coherence, because you have signaled that is the real scorecard.

None of this asks the company to slow down. It asks the company to prove it can go fast without coming apart, a higher bar than speed and the only one now worth setting. The agentic era will make your enterprise into one of two things: an organization you could have designed, or one that assembled itself from local decisions nobody chose in full view. Which one you get is the decision with your name on it, and no one else’s.​

#3174. Move Over, Amazon! Billionaire David Tepper of Appaloosa Has a New No. 1 Holding.

Appaloosa’s billionaire boss pared down dual-industry leader Amazon for a foundational company in the artificial intelligence (AI) data center build-out.

By Sean Williams – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:06AM EST

With the exception of earnings season, few data dumps are more valuable to investors than the quarterly filing of Form 13Fs with regulators. A 13F allows investors to track which stocks Wall Street's brightest and most successful money managers purchased and sold in the latest quarter (in this instance, during the third quarter).

Billionaire David Tepper, who oversees nearly $7.6 billion in assets under management at Appaloosa, is among Wall Street's most revered fund managers -- and he was a busy bee in the third quarter. Tepper modestly pared down what had been his fund's top holding, dual-industry leader Amazon (AMZN +0.37%), and bulked up Appaloosa's stake in another foundational artificial intelligence (AI) stock, Micron Technology (MU -5.35%).

Appaloosa's David Tepper was a busy bee in the third quarter. Image source: Getty Images.

According to Appaloosa's newest 13F, its billionaire boss disposed of 525,000 shares of Amazon, reducing his fund's remaining stake to 4,475,000 shares. Nevertheless, it still accounts for roughly 15% of Appaloosa's invested assets.

Tepper's modest selling may be due to simple profit-taking. Appaloosa has been a continuous shareholder of Amazon stock for more than seven years, with shares effectively tripling over that time.

But it's also possible that Tepper is concerned about Amazon's aggressive capital expenditures (capex) tied to the AI infrastructure build-out. The company logged a staggering free cash outflow of $33.4 billion during the September-ended quarter, with capex more than doubling from the comparable quarter in 2025. If fundamentals come back into focus, Amazon (and other hyperscalers) could take it on the chin.

However, for investors playing the long game, it's been business as usual for Amazon. In addition to dominating online retail sales, revenue growth in its higher-margin cloud infrastructure services segment, Amazon Web Services (AWS), is accelerating. The integration of generative AI and large language model solutions lifted AWS's year-over-year sales growth to 39% in the third quarter.

Whereas Appaloosa's billionaire chief reduced his fund's stake in Amazon by 10%, he scooped up another 275,000 shares of memory and storage solutions leader Micron Technology, increasing the position by 28% to 1,250,000 shares from the June-ended quarter and making it the new No. 1 holding.

The (likely) lure for David Tepper is Micron's foundational position in the AI data center build-out. The company is a key provider of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is packaged with graphics processing units to transfer data at jaw-dropping speed.

Micron has benefited from two dynamics. Firstly, the overwhelming demand for HBM and solid-state drives has boosted its pricing power and enabled the company to lock in more than $100 billion in strategic customer agreements (SCAs) through 2030.

Secondly, despite the best efforts of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -3.48%), HBM supply shortages persist. Ongoing supply shortages are affording Micron exceptional pricing power and its highest-ever gross margin.

However, history has repeatedly shown that strong pricing power for commoditized tech products, such as memory, tends to be short-lived. While Micron's SCAs should be able to offset potential price weakness for the foreseeable future, historical factors point to earnings multiple compression and the possibility of an AI bubble-bursting event taking place.

#3173. History Says This Is What Happens to the Nasdaq After the Midterms

Political uncertainty has been a source of volatility for stocks recently, and a striking historical trend could hint at what comes next.

By Keith Noonan – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›

The stock market has been volatile lately due to a series of macroeconomic risk factors and concerns about valuations for the companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry that has been so central to the market's gains in recent years.

Along those lines, some investors are worried that big wins for the Democratic Party in the recent U.S. midterm elections could impede data center buildouts, lead to the introduction of new regulations, and put some leading players in the AI space under greater scrutiny.

Stocks could continue to face some bearish pressures in the near term, but investors shouldn't overreact to the possibility of political headwinds. In fact, history says that the stock market typically enjoys strong performance in the year following midterm elections.

Due in part to uncertainty connected to the implications of election results, the stock market has tended to see more volatility and produce weaker returns in years that play host to midterm elections. Conversely, the year of trading following midterm elections has tended to produce strong returns.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has delivered an average return of 15% in the year of trading following midterms. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite has posted an average annual return of nearly 26% in post-midterm years since its founding in 1971. That kind of historical backdrop could suggest that now is a worthwhile time to put some investment dollars into the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -0.93%) -- an exchange traded fund (ETF) that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index and includes the 100 largest non-financials companies on the Nasdaq exchange.

On the other hand, it's important to keep in mind that past performance is no guarantee of future results. There are some unique dynamics on the table right now that could cause a divergence from typical post-midterm stock market trends next year.

For starters, inflation has continued to run relatively hot -- and there's a fair chance that the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will vote for an interest rate increase this year and at least one additional rate hike next year. Higher interest rates help to combat inflation, but they also create a less favorable backdrop for the stock market -- and growth stocks in particular. Adding additional macroeconomic pressures, bond yields have remained stubbornly high.

Massive valuation gains for leading AI companies including Nvidia, Alphabet, and Microsoft in recent years also mean that indexes including the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have become increasingly concentrated in recent years. This means that an investment in the Invesco QQQ Trust would likely face strong valuation pressures if sentiment surrounding top AI names shifts in a more bearish direction.

In summary, the historical trend suggests that the Nasdaq Composite, the Nasdaq 100, and the Invesco QQQ Trust should see strong returns in the year to come -- but investors also shouldn't treat that outcome as a given.

#3171. Rocket Lab Missed on Q3 Earnings -- and That's Great News

Rocket Lab isn't profitable yet -- but it's on the right track.

By Rich Smith – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:27AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Rocket Lab ›

Rocket Lab (RKLB -2.61%) stock "missed earnings" last week, reporting losses nearly twice as bad as Wall Street had predicted. And then the stock shot up -- and kept going up. By the close of trading last Friday, Rocket Lab stock was up nearly 16% from where it began the week.

Heading into the earnings report, analysts forecast Rocket Lab would lose $0.07 per share on sales of $257.2 million. Actual losses were $0.12 per share, however. Rocket Lab reported $268 million in Q3 sales, beating on that metric -- and it looks like there may be more gains in store.

Revenue hit a new quarterly record, rising 73% year over year to $268 million. Backlog of work to be done, however (i.e., future revenue), grew by nearly 6x that number -- $1.2 billion -- bringing the total backlog to $3.6 billion.

As fast as Rocket Lab grew in Q3, this massive backlog implies it's going to grow even faster in the future.

Also important is CEO Sir Peter Beck's observation that the company signed $470 million in Space Systems contracts and "nearly $1 billion" in new launch contracts in the quarter.

Why is this important? Consider that, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Rocket Lab's Launch Services division earned 43% gross profit margins over the last 12 months, while Space Systems earned closer to 33.6%. That's nearly a 10-percentage-point difference in profitability between Rocket Lab's two main divisions, with the advantage currently going to Launch Services -- which is outselling Space Systems 2-to-1!

So what does that mean for Rocket Lab? Not only will revenue growth accelerate, but the profits Rocket Lab earns on that revenue will accelerate even more (thanks to a higher profit margin).

And the good news doesn't end there. Rocket Lab generated positive operating cash flow in Q3 2026 -- $7.2 million. It's not a big number. It's not positive free cash flow. But this is the first time Rocket Lab has generated positive operating cash flow for a full quarter. Once it grows beyond capital investment costs, Rocket Lab will finally become FCF-positive.

I have publicly predicted that Rocket Lab will turn generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) profitable and FCF positive in 2027 after it completes its acquisition of Iridium Communications and adds Iridium's revenue and profit streams to its own.

In the meantime, Rocket Lab's Q4 guidance will show steady progress toward its goal. Turning to guidance, management predicts quarterly revenue between $270 million and $290 million, with gross margins from Launch Services and Space Systems blending to average 34%-36%.

This implies gross profit of about $98 million for the quarter. If operating costs reach $168 million -- as management also predicts -- this will prevent Rocket Lab from turning profitable in Q4. I'd similarly expect operating cash flow to be eclipsed by capital spending costs, which are averaging more than $30 million per quarter right now -- so you can expect no FCF in Q4, either.

All that said, Rocket Lab is on the right trajectory for profit. Sales are rising, profit margins are rising too, and Rocket Lab has demonstrated that it can generate positive operating cash flow. All it needs now is to scale that up past capital requirements. Once Iridium Communications is brought in-house, I expect that mission to be accomplished.

At a valuation of 44 times sales, Rocket Lab stock still looks pretty expensive to me, and I won't necessarily be buying more of it at this level. But as for how Rocket Lab is performing as a business?

#3170. Why Most Third-Party Risk Programs Are Taking The Wrong Measurements

Girish Redekar is Co-founder and CEO of Sprinto, building the future of trust for high-growth companies.

​I have answered security questionnaires as a vendor and sent them out as a buyer. On both sides, they do something useful: They surface what you cannot learn about a company from the outside.

The trouble starts when the questionnaire becomes the risk program instead of being one input to it.

A vendor tells you they enforce MFA, patch critical vulnerabilities within a defined SLA and encrypt customer data. All useful. But none of those answers tells you whether privileged access has drifted since. Or that the vendor shipped an AI feature last Tuesday, and your customer data now passes through a model provider you have never reviewed.

Every one of those answers can still be accurate. The questionnaire tells you what the vendor’s controls were designed to do. Your risk program needs to know what is actually happening today.

Measuring vendor risk only through questionnaires has a well-known flaw: The vendor grades themselves. But there are two other flaws that do more damage.

The first is age. A questionnaire is like the fire safety certificate framed in a restaurant lobby: accurate on the day it was issued. If you review vendors once a year, that snapshot guides your decisions for the next 12 months.

The second is that very different vendors often get pushed through versions of the same process. The payroll provider with salary data for your entire company and the tool your design team uses for designing mockups can end up answering much of the same questionnaire and landing in the same folder marked approved.

Some teams respond by sending the questionnaire every quarter instead of every year. I understand the instinct, but it gets them the same snapshot four times as often. AI makes this even easier, with vendors using it to fill out questionnaires and buyers using it to grade them. The paperwork moves faster, but what changed after approval is still invisible.

Imagine a vendor passes review in March. In August, your sales team connects it to the CRM, and it starts holding customer records. Nobody reviews the change because the vendor is already approved. In November, the vendor discloses a breach, and you find out your customer data was part of it.

The analyst who approved the vendor can show you a complete file. Her work ended at approval. The eight months after it fell between teams.

A questionnaire tells you what a vendor says should be true. You also need evidence of what is changing around that vendor. That is what I mean by exposure evidence.

Most of that evidence comes from how the business runs after approval. A tool approved for marketing gets rolled out to sales and starts holding pipeline data. The vendor switches on an AI feature by default in a routine update. Neither change passes back through procurement, and an external security score could miss both because nothing visible from the outside changed.

Continuous monitoring is what makes those signals useful. It watches for changes that alter the risk you originally accepted: a broader permission, a new use case, more sensitive data or access that should have expired. It also tells you which changes need attention and which do not, so you are not sending every vendor back through the same review.

All of it serves one decision: If this vendor came up for approval today, with what you now know, would you still approve it?

A board member asks a simple question: If one of our vendors were breached tomorrow, how exposed are we?

You might refer to the approval status: Every critical vendor was reviewed this year, and every one passed. That is a true statement about last spring.

A better answer sounds like this: Two vendors expanded into systems holding customer data this quarter, and both were re-reviewed. One switched on an AI feature that sends data to an outside model provider, so we reopened the assessment and restricted its use while we review the change. Here is what we are watching next quarter.

The second answer takes three minutes and gives the board something to act on.

If I had to replace questionnaire completion rates with a single number, it would be the days between a change at a critical vendor and someone on your team knowing about it. On an annual review cycle, that can be months.

You can start shrinking that number this week. List the 10 vendors that hold your customer data or touch production, and name one person who owns changes to each. Then ask that person what has changed at each vendor since it was last approved. If they have to email the vendor to find out, that gap is your answer.

The certificate in the lobby will keep saying the restaurant passed inspection. It won’t tell you someone stacked boxes in front of the fire exit last week. Your program should be measuring how quickly you notice.​

#3169. Bitwise CIO Predicts Hyperliquid Could Become "the Next Amazon." Here's Why He's Right.

One of Hyperliquid's strengths is that it gets other people to pay to broaden and deepen the markets on its platform.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Hyperliquid ›

When speaking on a podcast earlier this month, Matt Hougan, chief investment officer of crypto asset manager Bitwise, said that he thinks Hyperliquid (HYPE -9.37%) could become the next Amazon (AMZN +0.37%) thanks to its habit of expanding beyond crypto perpetual futures into real-world assets and prediction markets. That stance meshes cleanly with the view of Hyperliquid Labs' co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Jeff Yan, who wants it to become the "house all of finance." His preferred method for accomplishing that goal closely mirrors Amazon's marketplace model, in which sellers use the company's infrastructure to connect with their target buyers, facilitating transactions from which the platform takes a cut of the proceeds.

Hougan is probably correct about Hyperliquid's potential. Here's why, and how realizing that potential is likely to play out.

Hyperliquid is a decentralized exchange that specializes in perpetual futures contracts, or perps, which are a type of financial derivative. Users pay fees to trade them, and nearly all of the resulting revenue is used to buy back HYPE coins on the open market, like a stock buyback. The exchange earned $72.6 million in revenue during the 30-day period ended Nov. 19, and its coin is up by about 75% during the past 12 months.

Third-party merchants do much of Amazon's selling. Hyperliquid's equivalent is letting other companies commit the capital that's needed to create new markets on its platform, using its infrastructure. For now, new perpetuals markets and prediction markets are supported on Hyperliquid, and to launch one, a developer must stake 500,000 HYPE, worth about $34.4 million as of Nov. 19, which must stay locked for at least 183 days and can be rejected by validators if the market developer misbehaves. Then, those third parties are entitled to a portion of the fees generated by trading on the markets they funded.

Hyperliquid also offers a marketplace of "vaults." Vaults let anyone with $100 open an investment fund that others can invest in, almost like a mini hedge fund. The fund's manager is entitled to their portion of the fund's profits, and investors can easily screen hundreds of vaults to find those with the performance record and asset mix they prefer.

So in many ways, Hyperliquid is already following Amazon's business plan within its own domain.

As of October, more than 261 decentralized crypto exchanges offering perpetual futures trading have launched since Hyperliquid opened in 2022. But it still holds a 57% share of open interest in perps (the value of contracts outstanding) across decentralized perpetual futures exchanges.

This is to say that Hyperliquid's competitors are myriad and growing in number, and have always been so, and likely always will be. Plus, there are many powerful competitors aiming to achieve much the same outcome as Hyperliquid using other approaches. That means its margins may always be under pressure, and its growth may always be contested by competitors.

But the same was also true for Amazon in its early days, and that didn't stop it. So while it's probably not for the best to bet the farm on Hyperliquid becoming the Amazon of decentralized finance, it's certainly on track to accomplish just that.

#3168. What to Buy (and Skip) on Black Friday 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Electronics, small appliances, toys and clothes make the list, along with some out-of-the-box buys.

Black Friday comes but once a year — although sometimes it feels like it lasts for a month. The big day is Nov. 27, but the sales have already started.

If you’ve been sitting on a holiday shopping list and waiting for prices to drop, we’ve got good news: It’s time to start your shopping engines! (So to speak.)

You don’t need a calendar full of sale dates to navigate the shopping frenzy. Focus on the categories likely to offer the biggest savings. Here’s what to buy, and what can wait.

If you’ve got top-priority toys on your list, buy them at a discount if you can find them, says Kristin McGrath, senior editor at The Krazy Coupon Lady, “just in case they don’t go down in price later.”

Non-electronic toys are a good bet, says Julie Ramhold, consumer analyst with DealNews.com, because they’re less affected by tariffs on electronic components. That includes Legos, dolls and playsets.

NeeDoh squishies are a hot stocking stuffer this year and may be in short supply. At authorized retailers like Target, they should be relatively affordable, but try to avoid unauthorized resellers who may crank up the price, Ramhold says.

While you may see mattress stores offering a few doorbusters on Black Friday, don’t feel pressured to jump on a deal.

“Mattresses tend to see some of their strongest discounts around major sales events like Labor Day and Presidents Day,” says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, shopping and savings strategist with Rakuten. “So if you’re not in a rush, it may be worth waiting for one of those windows.”

Similarly, bedding and towels are often on deep discount during January white sales, Feinstein Gerstley says.

Got some counter space and an itch for a new food processor? Black Friday sales are a great time to price surf for countertop appliances, including blenders, juicers and air fryers.

“Those things we see sometimes half off or more,” McGrath says. “And they’re all on sale at the same time, so any one you’re looking for is likely to have a discount.”

Holiday decor is only a must-buy during Black Friday sales if you need it for this holiday season.

While you’ll still see sales on holiday items like artificial trees, drinkware and garlands, “if you can wait until after Christmas, that’s when discounts should reach up to 80% or more at stores like Target, Walmart and department stores like JCPenney and Macy’s,” Ramhold says.

Electronics are typically a slam-dunk buy at this time of year. “Every store is competing for your business, so televisions, headphones, tablets, laptops — they’re all going to be on sale at the same time,” McGrath says.

Gaming consoles, in particular, see some of the better discounts. And they often come bundled with a gift card, gaming accessories or video games. “Consoles are common gifts,” McGrath says. “The stores know that, so they’re offering competitive deals.”

That said, the traditional deep discounts you usually see on electronics for Black Friday may be a little lackluster this year due to high prices on parts, Ramhold says.

For best results, research the exact specs of the product you want and put it in your cart ahead of time, says consumer savings expert Andrea Woroch. That way, if a similar (but not identical) product goes on sale, you won’t accidentally buy the wrong thing.

You’ll usually find deeper discounts on items that are associated with fitness resolutions after New Year’s Day.

“Big-box retailers like Target and department stores like Macy’s will offer up to 40% off or more on both fitness equipment and activewear during early January sales,” Ramhold says.

Many fashion retailers offer Black Friday sales, McGrath says. So if there’s an item you stock in multiple colors or a work staple you need to replace, keep an eye on your favorite sites for the markdowns.

Shoes, too, are a category to eyeball, including seasonal buys and everyday options like running shoes, Ramhold says. “Some retailers may offer a BOGO promotion of some kind, but it’ll likely just be a ‘buy one, get one for 50% off,’” she says.

Just shop early for your size and color before inventory runs low, McGrath says. “You don’t want to miss out if there's a great deal.”

One caveat: Winter apparel will usually see bigger discounts toward the end of the year, Woroch says. So wait on your boot and coat purchases if you can.

Black Friday also offers the chance to snag deals on things you can use throughout the year:

Photo gifts: Whether you’re ordering holiday cards or putting together a photo book for your in-laws (or yourself), you can usually find sales from vendors like Snapfish and Shutterfly, among others.

Fitness classes: Try your local gym, yoga or Pilates studio for discounts on class packs. “I’ll buy a 20-class package, and it’s always a great deal,” Woroch says.

Spa services: Check local businesses for deals on massages, manicures and other self-care treatments.

Streaming subscriptions: If you’re a new customer (or canceled at least a month ago), some streaming platforms offer deep Black Friday discounts.

Black Friday deals are as much about strategy as savings, so make sure you’re maximizing your spending with these tips:

Let AI help. Tools like ChatGPT and Gemini can do a lot of the legwork for you. Write out a product name and try prompts like “Find the lowest price for X product by comparing every retail site that it’s sold on and including coupons and cash back offers,” Woroch says. (Just note that AI searches can be limited and may not find every deal available.)

Check the price, not just the percentage: “Sometimes the base price is inflated or it was listed initially for a higher price,” Feinstein Gerstley says. “Another retailer might have the same item for less, even if their discount doesn't look as impressive.”

Use a browser extension or cash-back app. As long as you’re spending money, recapture some of it with a browser extension or cash-back app that sends a percentage of your purchase back to you.
